tagline: Through the Absarokas, a winding road beside the Nez Perce Historic Trail
intro: Wyoming 296 winds through the Absaroka Mountains and Shoshone National Forest between the Beartooth Highway and Wyoming 120 north of Cody. The Wyoming Office of Tourism describes 47 paved miles through the mountains to the Clarks Fork Valley and advises allowing at least an hour to drive them. The Wyoming State Highway Commission designated the route as the Chief Joseph Scenic Highway in 1988. WYDOT describes a two-lane road with turnouts and picnic areas. Some stretches are steep and winding, with the Beartooth Mountains to the north and the Absarokas to the south.

The name recalls Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce Tribe, whose people fled through Yellowstone in 1877 while pursued by the U.S. Cavalry. They sought escape into Canada; the modern highway follows their route out of Yellowstone toward Montana. Along the byway, interpretive signs explain Chief Joseph’s history, and distinctive markers identify the parallel Nez Perce Historic Trail.

Start at U.S. 212 in the Clarks Fork Valley and follow 296 southeast through the forest. The road crosses Sunlight Creek on Wyoming’s highest bridge, then passes over Dead Indian Pass before reaching Wyoming 120. At the summit overlook, a paved turnout gives views of the Absaroka and Beartooth mountains.

moments.title: Clarks Fork of the Yellowstone
moments.text: The byway gives a view into the Clarks Fork gorge, where the river has cut rock as deep as 1,200 feet. The river crosses state lines, rising in Montana, flowing southeast into Wyoming’s Shoshone National Forest, then turning northeast into Montana again. In 1990, a 20.5-mile section in Wyoming entered the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System with a Wild designation. That section begins just below the Highway 296 bridge and extends downstream to near the western end of Canyon Road. The full river runs 150 miles before joining the Yellowstone southeast of Laurel, Montana.

moments.title: Sunlight Creek Bridge
moments.text: Pedestrian walkways flank the roadway on Sunlight Creek Bridge, a steel beam crossing over Sunlight Gorge. It is Wyoming’s highest bridge, spanning a gorge the creek carved 285.4 feet deep. The Wyoming Department of Transportation’s byway brochure identifies a highway pullout for a closer view of the bridge. The creek begins in the Absaroka Range and flows east through Sunlight Basin before entering its granite canyon. Beyond the bridge, it turns northeast to join the Clarks Fork Yellowstone River. In spring and summer, melting mountain snow feeds larger streams and tributaries that pour into Sunlight Creek.
moments.notice: Walkways run along both sides of the bridge above the creek-cut gorge.

moments.title: Dead Indian Pass
moments.text: At Dead Indian Pass, the byway crosses the Absaroka Range. The summit overlook provides a paved turnout with views across the Absaroka and Beartooth mountains. The pass is associated with the Nez Perce flight of 1877. The highway’s interpretive signs explain Chief Joseph’s significance, while markers distinguish the Nez Perce Historic Trail that parallels the road. Sunlight Basin lies below the western side of the pass. A pullout at the first switchback below the summit gives a view into the Clarks Fork Yellowstone River canyon. Dead Indian Creek runs at the base of the pass.
